         elsif cv.is_a?(Array)

+        elsif cv == true || cv == false
+          (cv ? 1 : 0) <=> (other_param.comparison_value ? 1 : 0) # <=> not defined for booleans, so convert to integer
body:
In this boolean branch, `other_param.comparison_value ? 1 : 0` relies on Ruby truthiness rather than ensuring the other value is actually boolean. If `other_param.comparison_value` is ever a non-boolean (e.g., an Integer like 0, or a String), it will be treated as `true` and can produce an incorrect / inconsistent ordering. Consider explicitly checking/casting `other_param.comparison_value` to `T::Boolean` (or TrueClass/FalseClass) before converting to 0/1 so mixed-type comparisons either sort deterministically or fail loudly.
```suggestion
          other_cv = other_param.comparison_value
          other_bool =
            if other_cv == true
              true
            elsif other_cv == false
              false
            else
              raise TypeError, "Expected comparison_value to be boolean, got #{other_cv.class}"
            end
          (cv ? 1 : 0) <=> (other_bool ? 1 : 0) # <=> not defined for booleans, so convert to integer
```

This branch raises a generic `RuntimeError` on type mismatch (`raise "Expected boolean ..."`). Elsewhere in this method type mismatches are surfaced via `T.cast` (which raises `TypeError` with a consistent message). Consider using `T.cast(other_param.comparison_value, T::Boolean)` (and optionally `T.cast(cv, T::Boolean)`) and raising `TypeError` explicitly if you still want a custom message, to keep failure modes consistent.

body: In the Array comparison branch, `cv <=> ...` will still raise when the array contains booleans (e.g., `equal: [true, false]`), since `TrueClass/FalseClass` don’t implement `<=>` and `Array#<=>` delegates to element `<=>`.
